name: Trofinetide
evidenceNote: Trofinetide was FDA-approved in 2023 as the first treatment for Rett syndrome, based on the 187-person randomized, placebo-controlled LAVENDER trial and earlier phase 2 work.
summary: The first approved drug for Rett syndrome, an oral analog of a tiny piece of IGF-1. FDA-approved since 2023; diarrhea is very common.
keyTakeaway: Trofinetide is a synthetic version of glycine-proline-glutamate, a three amino acid fragment of the growth factor IGF-1, taken by mouth twice a day. In March 2023 the FDA approved it as Daybue, the first treatment for Rett syndrome, for patients aged 2 and up. In the 12-week LAVENDER trial it improved caregiver and clinician ratings of Rett symptoms more than placebo, though the effects were small to moderate. Diarrhea affected about 82% of treated patients. The EU authorised it, as Daybu, in August 2026 for ages 5 and older.

blocks.text: Trofinetide is a drug for Rett syndrome, a rare genetic disorder of brain development [1] that affects communication, walking, hand use, attention, breathing, and seizure control [5]. Chemically it is a lab-made copy, slightly altered, of GPE (glycine, proline, glutamate), the three amino acids that open the chain of the growth factor IGF-1 [1].

It is sold in the United States by Acadia Pharmaceuticals as Daybue, an oral solution, and as Daybue STIX, a powder mixed into liquid [2][3]. It is swallowed or given through a gastrostomy (stomach) tube twice a day, with the dose set by body weight [2]. In the European Union the same drug is authorised under the name Daybu [8].

The honest answer is that no one knows exactly. The FDA label states plainly that the way trofinetide produces its effects in Rett syndrome is unknown [2]. It was chosen because it is derived from IGF-1 [1], but how that origin turns into changes in symptoms has not been worked out.

It is given by mouth or feeding tube, not by injection [2]. Its effect showed a dose relationship in early testing: in the pediatric phase 2 trial, only the highest dose clearly beat placebo, and improvement tracked with how much drug reached the blood [4].

That phase 2 study enrolled 82 girls aged 5 to 15, who received placebo or one of three doses for six weeks [4]. All three doses were well tolerated, and the top dose of 200 mg/kg twice a day improved the caregiver questionnaire, a clinician rating of key concerns, and the global impression score compared with placebo [4]. Those results set up the larger LAVENDER trial [5].

Yes. The FDA approved Daybue on March 10, 2023, as a new molecular entity with priority review and orphan drug status [3]. It is labeled for Rett syndrome in adults and children aged 2 years and older [2]. Label updates followed in 2024, 2025, and 2026, including a change backed by new clinical data in March 2026 [3].

Open-label extensions LILAC and LILAC-2 report up to 32 more months of use [6][7].
EU marketing authorisation for Daybu, ages 5 and older [8].

blocks.text: Trofinetide has one labeled use: Rett syndrome [2]. The trials measured changes in core symptoms such as behavior, communication, and overall clinical picture [1]. The EU authorisation is narrower in age, covering the neurobehavioural symptoms of Rett syndrome in patients aged 5 and older [8].

Approval rested on LAVENDER, a 12-week trial in 187 girls and women aged 5 to 20 who were randomly assigned to trofinetide or placebo [1][5]. Both main measures favored the drug. On the Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire, a caregiver-rated scale, scores fell by 4.9 points against 1.7 on placebo, and clinicians' global ratings were modestly better too [1]. The effect sizes were small to moderate (0.37 to 0.47) [1]. On a key secondary measure of communication and social skills, scores held steady with trofinetide (down 0.1) while they slipped by 1.1 on placebo [1].

blocks.text: Longer follow-up is uncontrolled. In LILAC, 154 participants continued for 40 weeks, and caregiver scores kept improving [6]. In LILAC-2, 77 participants stayed on for up to 32 more months; scores improved by 11.8 points from the original baseline at week 104, and most caregivers interviewed were satisfied [7]. Without a placebo group, these extensions cannot separate drug effect from expectation or natural change.

Diarrhea is by far the most common side effect, affecting 82% of patients on the drug against 20% on placebo in the label's trial data, and vomiting affected 29% against 12% [2]. The label tells families to stop laxatives before starting and to pause, lower, or stop the drug if diarrhea becomes severe or dehydration is suspected [2]. In the 40-week extension, diarrhea was the leading reason people stopped, in 21.4% of participants [6].

The other two warnings are weight loss, which calls for regular weight checks, and vomiting, which has led to aspiration and aspiration pneumonia in some patients [2]. Less common effects included fever, seizures, anxiety, reduced appetite, and fatigue [2]. People with moderate kidney impairment receive lower doses, and the drug is not recommended in severe kidney impairment [2].
